summary: Defines the forwarding element model for ForCES, which describes a forwarding element's functions, capabilities, state and configuration, and how those functions connect. Control elements use it to control the forwarding elements. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a blueprint of a worker machine, so the boss knows what it can do and how to set it up.

questions: how does forces describe an fe
what is a logical functional block
what is the forces forwarding element model
subtitle: A common blueprint for describing what a packet-forwarding box can do, how it is wired inside, and how a controller can configure it.

tldr.problem: In ForCES a control element configures separate forwarding elements that may differ widely in functionality, so the controller needs a standard way to discover what each one can do and what state it is in.
tldr.mechanism: The model breaks an FE into Logical Functional Blocks wired into a directed graph, passing packets and metadata. Each block class is defined in an XML schema with ports, components, capabilities and events, and a single FE Object block describes the FE as a whole.
tldr.outcome: The model supplies the vocabulary the ForCES protocol uses to query and configure forwarding elements, but defines only the FE Object block itself. Other block classes are left to other documents.

facts.label: Identifier size
facts.value: 32 bits for FE, class, instance and component IDs

today: RFC 5812 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7408. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why ForCES Needs a Forwarding Element Model
sections.content:
The ForCES framework (RFC 3746) lets control elements (CEs) configure and manage one or more separate forwarding elements (FEs) inside a network element. FEs can differ in functionality, so a CE can make only minimal assumptions about them. Before it can control forwarding, a CE has to query and discover each FE's capabilities and state, and RFC 3654 requires that these be expressed as an FE model.

RFC 5812 is that model. It is described as primarily an information model, though it also includes parts of a data model, such as explicit definitions of the LFB class schema and FE schema. It is expected to be the basis for the payload that CEs and FEs exchange in the ForCES protocol (RFC 5810).

The model has to describe the separable packet forwarding operations in an FE (Logical Functional Blocks), how they can be connected, the capabilities and configurable parameters of each, and the metadata passed between them. It is not meant to say how a given implementation maps onto the model. That is left to forwarding plane vendors.
sections.eli5: A boss who runs many different machines needs to ask each one what it can do before giving orders. This RFC is the list of questions and answers they all agree to use.

sections.title: Capabilities, State and Logical Functional Blocks
sections.content:
The model separates three things: capabilities (what an FE can or cannot do, including capacity limits such as table sizes), state (what it is doing now) and configuration (what the CE wants it to be). Capabilities and state flow from FE to CE, and configuration flows from CE to FE. The RFC chooses coarse capability reporting combined with error reporting: if the CE asks for something the FE cannot do, the FE returns an error.

The building block is the Logical Functional Block (LFB). Each LFB performs a well-defined action on packets, such as classifying, metering, shaping or marking, and typically does a single action. Fine-grained blocks let a small number of block types express higher-level functions such as an IPv4 forwarder. A block may also exist only to hold components for control, like the FE Object, and then has no packet-oriented properties.

An LFB has inputs, outputs and components that the CE can query and change through the ForCES protocol. The model is made of three parts: the LFB models, the LFB topology (how blocks are connected) and FE-level attributes such as capabilities.
sections.eli5: Each machine in the factory does one small job, like sorting or stamping. The model lists each machine, what it could do, what it is doing now, and the knobs the boss may turn.

sections.title: Inputs, Outputs and Metadata
sections.content:
Every LFB input and output carries a pair: a packet and its metadata. Either one may be empty, but not both. Metadata is per-packet state passed from one LFB to another, modeled as a label and value pair (for example a color label with the value red). It is not sent across the network.

An output can feed only one input, so packet flow is unambiguous, but several outputs may feed the same input. To fork a data path, a class can have multiple singleton outputs (a fixed number of semantically different outputs, such as OUT and EXCEPTIONOUT) or an output group, where the number of paths is not known when the class is defined. Fan-in has three forms: a single shared input, multiple singleton inputs, or an input group, where the LFB knows which input instance a packet arrived on.

For each metadatum on a packet path there MUST be at least one producer LFB and there SHOULD be at least one consumer. Producers and consumers need not be adjacent, and later producers overwrite earlier values. A block can leave a metadatum alone, read it, rewrite it, create it, or consume it, which ends its life. The class definition must also list the packet types (such as IPv4, IPv6, Ethernet) each input accepts and each output emits.
sections.eli5: Each package moving down the conveyor belt carries a sticky note. Machines can read the note, change it, or tear it off. A machine can send packages down one belt or several, but each belt end only plugs into one place.

sections.title: Events, Versioning and Inheritance
sections.content:
LFB classes declare events, conditions the FE can detect and report to the CE, such as link failure or timer expiry. An event declaration has a unique 32-bit identifier, an event target component, a trigger condition and a declared report. A CE subscribes at runtime by turning on a subscription property, which is off by default, and can add filters such as thresholds, hysteresis, time intervals and event counts. The format of event messages belongs to the ForCES protocol.

Classes evolve in two ways. Versioning requires a version string in each class definition. CEs may support several versions of a class, but FEs MUST NOT support more than one version of a particular class. Versions may make changes that inheritance cannot, such as correcting errors or removing components.

Inheritance defines new classes from a base class, which also lets vendors extend standardized blocks. A class MUST name its base class and version, and multiple inheritance is not allowed. A derived class must be a functional superset of its base, so it can add but not remove components. For backward compatibility, a CE MUST be able to query the base class of an unknown LFB, and an LFB SHOULD support a mode that reverts it to its base class.
sections.eli5: Machines can ring a bell when something happens, but only if the boss asked to hear it. New machine models can add buttons to an old one, but they must never remove the old buttons.

sections.title: Addressing Every Piece of the Model
sections.content:
Every construct has a 32-bit identifier. An FE has an FEID, each LFB class has a LFB ClassID that is global within the network element, each instance has an ID unique within its class on that FE, and each component within an instance has a component ID. A message can therefore be aimed at, for example, FE01, class 1, instance 3.

Components can be nested structures or tables, so the model uses dot-annotated paths. If component 51 is a structure holding component 89, the path is 51.89. If 51 is a table, the path to component 89 in the 7th entry is 51.7.89. Tables can also be declared with content keys, so a CE can select an entry by its contents rather than by position. Each key is built from one or more fields, and no two entries in a table instance may have the same key values.
sections.eli5: It is like a full postal address: country, street, house and then which room. Each part has its own number so anything can be found exactly.

sections.title: Data Paths and LFB Topology
sections.content:
The LFB topology is a directed graph of the logical data paths in an FE. Nodes are LFB instances and links show packet flow. It is the logical topology, not the physical layout of the hardware.

Differences in packet treatment can be modeled in two ways. The topological approach splits the graph into separate paths. The encoded state approach has a block write the result into metadata that downstream blocks use, for example as a table index. The RFC says neither alone fits every case. The topological approach suits forks to distinct LFB classes that rarely change, while frequently changing configuration should live in LFB attributes.

Topology may also be reconfigurable. This is not required of every FE, and performance-optimized hardware may have little or none. But a CE MUST be able to learn an FE's configuration capabilities, such as which LFB classes can be instantiated, how many instances, and ordering limits. The RFC's example is a QoS router where a classifier chip is hardwired in front of a programmable network processor holding meter, marker, dropper, counter, queue, scheduler and IPv4 forwarder blocks. The CE then maps its service policy onto a topology the FE accepts.
sections.eli5: You can build a factory with a separate belt for every kind of job, or with one belt and labels telling each machine what to do. Real factories mix both, and the boss is told which rearrangements are allowed.

sections.title: The XML Schema for LFB Class Libraries
sections.content:
LFB classes are defined in library documents, XML documents that must conform to the schema in the RFC and use the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:forces:lfbmodel:1.0. The root element is <LFBLibrary>. These definitions are a design reference and are not expected to be exchanged between FEs and CEs over the wire. The wire encoding is up to the ForCES protocol.

Optional top-level elements must appear in this order: description, load (like a C include of another library), frameDefs, dataTypeDefs, metadataDefs and LFBClassDefs. Built-in atomic types include uchar, uint16, uint32, boolean, string, byte[N] and float64. Compound types are arrays (fixed or variable size, optionally with content keys), structs and unions.

A class definition has a name, synopsis and version, and may include derivedFrom, inputPorts, outputPorts, components, capabilities, events and a description of its behavior. Capabilities are read-only. Properties attached to components cover things like readability, array bounds and event settings. The RFC also gives a worked example of a fictional optical interface LFB.
sections.eli5: Every machine type gets a spec sheet in a strict format: what it takes in, what it puts out, its settings and the sensors it has. Everyone writes the sheets the same way so they can be read by people and programs.

sections.title: The FE Object and Use in the Protocol
sections.content:
FE-wide information lives in an LFB of class FEObject, which has class ID 1 and exactly one instance, with instance ID 1. A CE can always read class 1, instance 1 to learn about the FE. Class ID 2 is reserved for an FEProtocol object defined in RFC 5810.

FEObject capabilities are ModifiableLFBTopology (whether the CE may change the topology; true if absent) and SupportedLFBs, a list of supported classes with instance limits, port group limits and which classes each can come before or after. Its components include FEState (values AdminDisable, OperDisable, OperEnable), the LFBSelectors list of instances, the optional LFBTopology of links, and optional FENeighbors. Links support fan-in but not fan-out.

The ForCES protocol uses the model for seven kinds of exchange: FE topology query, FE capability declaration, LFB topology and configurability query, LFB capability declaration, state query, component manipulation and topology reconfiguration. The model itself defines only the FE Object, and further LFB classes come from other documents. For security it relies on the ForCES framework, which requires protocol entities to be authenticated before accessing this information.
sections.eli5: Every factory has one special office desk with the factory's own info sheet. The boss always knows where to find it, and from there can learn about every machine.

viz.caption: WHAT AN LFB CAN DO TO A METADATUM (RFC 5812, SECTION 3.2.4.3)

items.label: Read and rewrite
items.desc: Reads, overwrites and forwards the metadatum.

items.label: Write
items.desc: Writes and forwards the metadatum; can also create new metadata.

items.label: Read and consume
items.desc: Reads the metadatum and ends its life cycle.

items.label: Consume
items.desc: Consumes the metadatum without reading it.
